findings.note: InitializeView at api/views/device.py:145. True as read: authentication_classes = () and permission_classes = (), routed for POST. It is pretix's device enrolment endpoint, the point at which a physical point-of-sale device trades a one-time initialization token for a long-lived API token, so it necessarily precedes authentication. The credential is checked in the handler -- Device.objects.get(initialization_token=...) raising ValidationError on an unknown token, with further refusals for tokens already used or revoked -- which is the hand-written check DJA-003 lists as invisible to it. Accepted rather than false positive for the same reason as NetBox's token provisioning: the statement is correct, and an anonymous POST endpoint earning one line of review is the rule working, not misfiring.

SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT is never assigned anywhere in src/pretix, so Django itself does not redirect plain HTTP. That is deliberate rather than an oversight: pretix expects TLS to be terminated in front of it, and the reference deployment in deployment/docker/nginx.conf listens on port 80 only and reverse-proxies to gunicorn over a unix socket, which means the Django process legitimately never sees a TLS connection to redirect from. The statement the rule makes is true and the redirect really is absent from this repository; where it happens is the operator's, not the developer's, decision. Recorded as accepted rather than a false positive for the same reason as the NetBox entries: whether the target chooses to handle something elsewhere says nothing about whether we were right to point at it.

SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS is never assigned, so Django sends no Strict-Transport-Security header. Same layering as DJS-006: pretix does not terminate TLS, and an HSTS header emitted by an application that is only ever reached over plaintext from its own reverse proxy would be both useless and, if the proxy ever forwarded it unchanged for a subdomain, actively harmful. The shipped nginx config does not set the header either, so a site following the reference deployment sends no HSTS at all -- which is a genuine gap, but one that belongs to the TLS terminator the operator supplies rather than to this codebase. Accepted rather than true_positive because there is no line in this repository whose change would fix it.

SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER = ('HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PROTO', 'https') at settings.py:242 sits inside `if config.getboolean('pretix', 'trust_x_forwarded_proto', fallback=False):` at line 241, so it is off unless an operator opts in through a config file that is not part of this repository, and the option is named for exactly the trust it establishes. The rule's point stands regardless of the guard -- once enabled, any client that can reach gunicorn directly can assert HTTPS by sending the header, so the proxy must overwrite rather than append it -- which is why this is reported at low/tentative and stays out of a default run. Accepted: the risk is real, opt-in, and named.

ALLOWED_HOSTS = ['*'] at settings.py:255 is unconditional. pretix needs to answer on organizer- and event-specific custom domains, so it cannot enumerate hosts ahead of time, and it resolves them itself in pretix.multidomain.middlewares.MultiDomainMiddleware. But that middleware does not reject an unrecognised host: on KnownDomain.DoesNotExist it sets mode='system' (middlewares.py:101-104) and serves the main site, so Django's host validation is disabled and nothing replaces it. deployment/docker/nginx.conf:89 forwards `Host $http_host` verbatim, so the header arrives unfiltered. That leaves the documented consequence intact -- absolute URLs, including password-reset links, are built from an attacker-supplied Host, and cache keys derived from it can be poisoned. Genuinely mitigable by pinning SITE_URL's host plus the KnownDomain set, so this is a real finding rather than an accepted trade-off.

True reading, and unavoidable for pretix. OrderPosition.secret is a 32-character random string (models/orders.py:254) that is the ticket: it is what the barcode encodes and what the scanning app checks at the door, so it is a bearer credential in the strict sense. OrderPositionSerializer returns it because every consumer of this API -- ticket rendering, resending an email, a check-in device -- needs the value to do anything useful. The protection is on the endpoint rather than the field: these serializers sit behind organizer-scoped permissions. Accepted as designed. The rule is still right to name it, because 'the API returns the thing that opens the gate' is exactly what a reviewer of a new integration needs told.

True reading. GiftCard.secret is the redemption code (models/giftcards.py:93) and is returned by __str__ as the card's public identity, so it is a bearer credential that pretix intends to be readable -- an organizer cannot hand out a gift card without it. Behind organizer permissions. Accepted as designed.

True reading, and the clearest example in the benchmark set of what this rule is for. OrderSerializer.positions = OrderPositionSerializer(many=True, read_only=True) is a plain nesting with no narrowing, so every order response embeds each position's full field list -- including secret, the 32-character string the ticket barcode encodes. A reviewer reading OrderSerializer's Meta.fields sees 'positions' and nothing that suggests credential material. pretix intends this: an integration fetching an order needs the ticket secrets to render or scan tickets, and the endpoint sits behind organizer-scoped permissions. Accepted as designed. The finding is still worth raising, because the parent's field list is the one people read.

True reading, same shape on the create path. OrderCreateSerializer.positions nests OrderPositionCreateSerializer, whose field list includes secret, so a create response returns the newly generated ticket secrets. This is how a caller learns the secrets for tickets it just created, which is the point of the endpoint. Accepted as designed.
